`services.confirm_operator_mfa_enrolment` for why re-presenting the same code through
`/mfa/verify` would be redundant. Recovery codes are shown once, exactly as the tenant
flow's are.
OperatorMfaEnrolled.title: OperatorMfaEnrolled

OperatorMfaEnrollmentRequired.description:
A staff account with no confirmed factor. There is no further path but enrolling one —
unlike the tenant flow, an operator cannot land here and simply keep going.
OperatorMfaEnrollmentRequired.title: OperatorMfaEnrollmentRequired

OperatorMfaRequired.description: A staff account with an already-confirmed factor must present it.
OperatorMfaRequired.title: OperatorMfaRequired

OperatorTokenOut.description:
A completed operator sign-in.

Carries `aud="operator"` and `stf=true` inside the token (not repeated here); the
refresh token is set as an httpOnly cookie, never in this body. `operator_roles` is
surfaced so the console can render without decoding the token.
OperatorTokenOut.title: OperatorTokenOut

SsoConfigIn.description:
The administrative form. **The secret goes in and never comes back.**

`client_secret` is optional on update: leaving it out keeps the stored one, so changing a
display name does not mean re-typing a credential.
SsoConfigIn.title: SsoConfigIn

SsoConfigOut.description:
What the console renders. Note the absence: there is no secret field at all.

Not a masked one either — a mask of a client secret is a hint about a credential and
buys the reader nothing they need. `client_secret_set` says whether one is stored, which
is the only question the form has to answer.
SsoConfigOut.title: SsoConfigOut

SsoStartOut.description:
Where to send the browser to authenticate.

JSON rather than a 302 because the caller is a single-page app: it needs to stash its own
return location before leaving, and a redirect the fetch layer follows invisibly gives it
nowhere to do that. `state` is echoed so the client can recognise its own callback; it is
not a credential — the value that matters is stored server-side against it, and it is
single-use.
SsoStartOut.title: SsoStartOut

TokenOut.description: A completed sign-in. No refresh token here — see the module docstring.
TokenOut.title: TokenOut

Exchange credentials for tokens, or for the next step.

Three outcomes: signed in, needs a second factor, or needs to pick an organization.
The organization comes from an explicit slug, the host the gateway saw, or a single
membership — never inferred from the email domain.

post.description:
A password alone must never be enough to reach MFA enrolment (ADR-0003 addendum): this
is the audited, in-product way an `owner` hands a colleague — or a newly provisioned staff
account — the out-of-band code `POST /auth/operator/mfa/enrol` also requires. For the very
first owner, with nobody yet to issue one, `bin/seed-staff` prints one instead; for staff
accounts that predate this rule, `bin/issue-enrollment-codes` is the one-off deploy step.
post.summary: Issue a staff account's out-of-band MFA enrolment code (owner only)

post.description:
Authenticate a staff account. Never returns a token from a password alone.

A wrong credential answers 401 with the same generic message the tenant login uses, so
this endpoint is not an operator-account enumeration oracle. A correct one always
returns one of two "keep going" answers — MFA is mandatory for staff (ADR-0003
addendum) — never a completed sign-in.

post.description:
Idempotent. Shares `services.logout`, which touches only the session and refresh
tables — no directory, so it ends an operator session as cleanly as a tenant one.

get.description:
Goes through the same tenancy chokepoint as every other principal-bearing route.

Harmless rather than meaningful for an operator: `get_tenant_session` binds the
transaction to `principal.organization_id`, which for an operator token is the platform
sentinel (`services.PLATFORM_ORG`) — there is no tenant row here to protect, `auth`
carries no row-level security at all, but going through the one chokepoint every
principal-bearing route uses is one fewer shape for this module to special-case.

post.summary: Start setting up an operator's authenticator app — the only reachable step until one is enrolled
Prove the app works — completes the sign-in that started enrolment

post.description:
The lost-device path (MINOR 5 of the 2026-09-24 security review): deletes the target's
factors and recovery codes, revokes their live sessions and refresh tokens, and audits the
act. Refuses to target the caller — resetting one's own MFA is not what this route is for.
Once this has run, `POST /auth/operator/enrollment-codes` issues the fresh out-of-band code
the account's next enrolment needs.
post.summary: Wipe a colleague's MFA after a lost device (owner only)

post.description:
Always accepted, whether or not the address exists.

A 404 here would tell whoever is asking which addresses are real, without them
guessing a single password.

post.summary: Set a new password from a reset link

post.description:
Rotate the refresh token and mint a new access token.

Presenting a token that was already rotated ends the whole family — see
`services.rotate_refresh` for why that trade is the right one.

get.description:
Where the identity provider sends the browser back.

Returns exactly what `POST /auth/login` returns on success — the same `TokenOut`, the
same httpOnly refresh cookie, a token minted by the same `issue_for`. That is deliberate:
a client should not be able to tell how somebody signed in from the shape of what it got,
because anything that branched on it would be a second code path to keep correct.

The redirect URI registered with the provider is this path, and it comes from
configuration (`sso_redirect_uri`) rather than from anything in the request — a redirect
target a caller can influence is how an authorization code ends up somewhere else.

put.description:
Create or replace the OIDC configuration.

Whoever holds `core.identity.sso.write` decides which external issuer may assert who
their colleagues are, and can turn password sign-in off for everyone — which is why it is
ORG-scoped and, in the catalogue, marked dangerous.

get.description:
Resolve the identity provider for a domain and hand back its authorization URL.

The domain is what selects a *provider*, and only a domain the organization proved it
owns (ADR-0000 §1). Every way this can fail answers the same 404 with the same message,
so it cannot be used to enumerate which domains, organizations or configurations exist.
get.summary: Begin single sign-on for an email domain

post.description: Move a live session to another organization, keeping the same session id.

get.description:
How far behind the relay is. **Alert on `oldest_seconds`.**

A stalled relay is the platform's quietest failure. It selects, finds nothing,
logs nothing, sleeps, and loops — `attempts` never increments and `last_error`
stays null, so the process looks healthy indefinitely while the outbox grows
without bound and every consumer downstream starves.

Deliberately **not** part of readiness. A backlog is not a reason to take the
service out of rotation: refusing traffic would stop new events being written
without helping drain the ones already queued, which makes the incident worse.
This is a metric to alert on, not a health state.

Counted through the outbox engine, not the application one. The app role is
NOBYPASSRLS and this request binds no tenant, so through it `pending` would be
zero whatever the table holds — the probe that exists to expose the stall would
be wired to the same blind spot that causes it.
get.summary: Outbox depth and age — scrape this

get.description:
Route traffic on this; restart on /health.

Conflating the two restarts a healthy process that is merely waiting on a
dependency.

Only the dependencies a service actually declares are checked. A gateway owns no
tables, so asking it for a database is asking a question whose answer means nothing
— and a readiness probe that reports on something the service does not use is worse
than no probe, because it will eventually fail for a reason nobody can act on.
